stem: A research team sets out to review the evidence base for combining antidepressants to treat resistant depression. For the literature search to be complete which of the following strategy should not be followed?
options: Writing to experts for any missing studies
Cross checking reference list from identified studies
Avoiding conference posters as data may not be peer reviewed
correctAnswer: Avoiding conference posters as data may not be peer reviewed
explanation: A properly conducted literature search must have following properties: 1. Using multiple databases - not just limiting to MEDLINE only or CINAHL only. 2. Cross checking the references list of each individual study retrieved by direct search 3. Hand searching for materials unidentified online. 4. Approaching experts to comment on any missing studies. 5. Identifying grey literature" i.e. the unpublished literature such as conference abstracts, presentations and posters.

stem: While identifying the appropriate literature, the research team above finds 12 uncontrolled trials and 3 RCTs. Which of the following statement is true with regard to conducting a meta-analysis of above studies?
options: Meta-analysis is not feasible due to high publication bias
Meta-analysis may be weak as study designs are different
Meta-analysis can be performed but it will show a near zero effect side
Meta-analysis is not indicated as 3 RCTs already exist.
Meta-analysis cannot be performed as 15 studies are insufficient
correctAnswer: Meta-analysis may be weak as study designs are different
explanation: A meta-analysis is a statistical method of combining study results. It is best done using studies with a common methodology (all RCTs, all case-control studies), etc. But increasingly certain meta-analytical papers seem to override this tradition. Having small number of studies does not prevent, but weaken a meta-analysis. One cannot predict effect size of a meta-analysis without looking at the effects in individual  trials. One may find the degree of publication bias while conducting a meta-analysis; high degree of bias can make the effect of outcome questionable. But this will not stop one from attempting a meta-analysis. Some authors argue that meta-analyses pooling significantly heterogeneous studies have limited validity, though it is possible to combine studies of different methodologies. It is best to conduct 2 separate meta-analysis – one for RCTS and one for uncontrolled trials.

stem: The highest place in the hierarchy of evidence is given to which of the following studies?
options: A systematic review of several double-blind randomised control trials.
One or more large double-blind randomised control trials.
One or more well-conducted cohort studies.
One or more well-conducted case-control studies.
correctAnswer: A systematic review of several double-blind randomised control trials.
explanation: Hierarchy of evidence I-1 Systematic review of several double-blind randomised control trials. I-2 One or more large double-blind randomised control trials. II-1 One or more well-conducted cohort studies. II-2 One or more well-conducted case-control studies. II-3 A dramatic uncontrolled experiment. III Expert Committee sitting in review; peer leader opinion. IV Personal experience. 

stem: Which of the following is true with respect to impact factor
options: It refers to the quality of a scientific journal
It refers to the quality of an author
It refers to the quality of a scientific article
It is a static number that cannot be changed
It is sensitive to the subject area of a journal
correctAnswer: It refers to the quality of a scientific journal
explanation: The impact factor is a measure of the frequency with which the "average article" in a journal has been cited in a given period. The impact factor for a journal is calculated based on a three-year period, and can be considered to be the average number of times published papers are cited up to two years after publication (Retrieved from http://journalseeker.researchbib.com/). It is thus journal-specific and not article specific. 

stem: All of the following are natural steps in practising evidence-based medicine for a clinician except
options: Search and track down relevant evidence
Apply the evidence with consideration to patient's values
Calculating impact factor of the journal
correctAnswer: Calculating impact factor of the journal
explanation: The steps in evidence-based practice according to Glazsiou (2000) are 1. Formulate an answerable question. 2. Track down the best evidence of outcomes available. 3. Critically appraise the evidence (to find out how good it is and what it means). 4. Apply the evidence (integrate the results with clinical expertise and patient values). 

You know that the risk of this is recognised with fluoxetine but want to quote a precise number that he can understand. Which of the following population will you use as a comparator when formulating a query to search the literature
explanation: What would Stephen do if he didn't take fluoxetine (the intervention) - it is very likely that, in this case, he might not be on anything rather than taking phenelzine. It makes more sense to the patient when side effects are discussed in comparison to not taking an intervention  rather than taking an alternative intervention.

stem: Which of the following is presently the best resource to search for registered clinical trials?
explanation: At present, Cochrane register (Called CENTRAL) is an excellent resource for all registered clinical trials. One can even find information regarding on-going studies that are yet to be published.

stem: Which of the following measures is the most effective in making clinicians apply a new clinical guideline in their practice?
options: Discussing the guidelines in academic meetings
Creating online educational modules for the guidelines
Using patient specific reminders related to the guidelines
Publishing guidelines in peer reviewed journal
correctAnswer: Using patient specific reminders related to the guidelines
explanation: Adherence with evidence-based recommendations for chronic disease management is often suboptimal. Providing patient-specific reminders at the time of clinical encounters has the potential to improve this situation (Retrieved from http://www.nature.com/ebd/journal/v2/n3/full/6400038a.htm). 

stem: Which of the following provides a consensus statement for reporting systematic reviews?
explanation: Guidelines have now been published that should improve the reporting of clinical trials (CONSORT) and systematic reviews (QUORUM). These guidelines make it easier to judge research quality and should improve peer review: conclusions from clinical trials or systematic reviews using these guidelines are more likely to be reliable ( Retrieved from http://www.nature.com/ebd/journal/v2/n3/full/6400038a.html). 

stem: Which of the following would be the most appropriate measure when explaining positive treatment response to patients?
explanation: Among the listed options, NNT is the best available tool to easily describe the benefits of a drug. But shortcomings of NNT include the lack of information regarding how long one needs a treatment and the adverse effects of a treatment. It does not convey how much better the patient will be after the treatment. Interestingly when a sample of the Danish population (n = 675) were asked whether they would consent to a hypothetical drug that reduces the risk of heart attack with the benefit of the drug expressed in terms of NNT randomly set at 10, 25, 50,  100, 200, and 400 etc., the proportion of people consenting to the hypothetical drug was observed to be about 80%, irrespective of NNT! Lay people may have difficulties in understanding the meaning of NNT, and clinicians may do well to use the NNT with caution until more is known about how patients comprehend it. Kristiansen IS, Gyrd-Hansen D, Nexoe J, et al. Number needed to treat: Easily understood and intuitively meaningful? Theoretical considerations and a randomized trial. J Clin Epidemiol 2002;55:888-92

stem: Which one of the following bodies is formed to generate consensus guidelines in relation to healthcare?
explanation: The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) is the independent organisation responsible for providing national guidance on the promotion of good health and the prevention and treatment of ill health. NICE produces guidance in three areas of health: public health, health technologies and clinical practice. 

stem: Which one of the following hierarchy is correct in evidence-based practice?
options: Qualitative research, systematic review, RCTs, non RCTs, cohort studies.
Meta analysis, Systematic review, RCT, Non RCT, Cohort, Case Control.
RCT, meta-analysis, cohort studies, case control studies, case reports.
RCT, Non RCT, Cohort Study, Case Control, Meta analysis
Expert opinion, narrative reviews, RCTs, Cohort studies
correctAnswer: Meta analysis, Systematic review, RCT, Non RCT, Cohort, Case Control.
explanation: The EBM hierarchy indicates the relative weight that can be attributed to a particular study design. The higher up a methodology is ranked, the more robust it is assumed to be. At one end lies the meta-analysis, synthesizing the results of a number of similar trials to produce a result of higher statistical power. At the other end of the spectrum lie observational studies thought to provide the weakest level of evidence. (From public-health-textbook issues by DoH - http://www.healthknowledge.org.uk) 

stem: Which one of the following is considered as a structured way to formulate a question when practising Evidence-Based Medicine ?
explanation: A structured way to formulate an EBM question is to specify the population, intervention, comparators and outcome, which are also known as the PICO format. This is a useful guideline for treatment studies but may not fit all questions.

stem: Which one of the following is correct with regard to the Cochrane library?
options: Cochrane library does not have articles on mental health research
Cochrane maintains a register of controlled trials
Cochrane project will be completed in 2010
All interventions studies are registered with the Cochrane
Cochrane is an alternative index to Medline
correctAnswer: Cochrane maintains a register of controlled trials
explanation: The Cochrane Library includes i. Regularly-updated systematic reviews and protocols for reviews in preparation prepared by the Cochrane collaboration of clinical researchers in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. ii. Quality appraisals of reviews published elsewhere are maintained in the Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effectiveness. iii. A register of controlled trials, in the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register. Cochrane collaboration runs a continuous process of systematic appraisal and synthesis of clinical evidence. It is not an alternative  to Medline. Despite the usefulness, not all intervention trials get registered in the Cochrane.

stem:
Economic analysis of clozapine An open-label, randomized controlled trial compared 10 patients on clozapine with 10 patients on physicians'-choice medications. 6 out of 10 patients on clozapine achieve remission while 5 out of 10 patients on other antipsychotics achieve remission. For each patient, clozapine costs 3000£ per course while other antipsychotics cost 1800£ per course. On the whole clozapine-treated group achieved 200 symptom-free months while the other group achieved 150 symptom-free months. Choose one of the above options for each of the following measures:

The cost per patient remitted on clozapine Choose...

The cost per patient remitted on other antipsychotics Choose...

The incremental cost of clozapine to achieve one additional remission Choose...

The incremental cost of clozapine per symptom-free month gained Choose...
correctAnswer: The cost per patient remitted on clozapine → 5000£, The cost per patient remitted on other antipsychotics → 3600£, The incremental cost of clozapine to achieve one additional remission → 12000£, The incremental cost of clozapine per symptom-free month gained → 240£
explanation: 1) For 10 patients taking clozapine 3000*10 = 30,000£ are spent i.e. for 6 remissions 30,000 therefore for one remission 30,000/6 = 5000£. 2) For 10 patients taking other antipsychotics 1800*10 = 18,000£ are spent i.e. for 5 remissions 18,000 therefore for one remission 18,000/5 = 3600£. 3) For one additional patient to remit we need to treat 10 patients with clozapine compared to 10 patients with other antipsychotics (i.e. 6 - 5 = 1). The incremental cost is then 30,000 - 18000 = 12,000£. 4) In total 50 months (200-150) are gained by spending 12,000 additional ££. 12,000/50 = 240£ needed for each additional month of remission.

stem:
Fluoxetine for BDD In a multicentre, double-blind RCT with well-concealed allocation, fluoxetine 20mg was compared to placebo for 200 patients with body dysmorphic disorder. Outcomes (improved vs. not improved in BDD scale) were measured after three months and six months of treatment. 100 patients received fluoxetine while 100 patients received placebo. At six months, 75 patients on fluoxetine improved compared to 25 patients receiving placebo. For ethical reasons further follow-up was avoided, and the placebo group received fluoxetine afterwards. Calculate the following measures using the below study data:

The chance that a patient receiving placebo treatment will improve at six months. Choose...

The odds of getting better while taking fluoxetine compared to placebo for six months. Choose...

The absolute benefit increase due to fluoxetine treatment. Choose...

The number of patients with body dysmorphic disorder that needs treatment to achieve one case of improvement. Choose...

The rate of improvement when taking fluoxetine. Choose... 
correctAnswer:
The chance that a patient receiving placebo treatment will improve at six months. → 25%, The odds of getting better while taking fluoxetine compared to placebo for six months. → 9, The absolute benefit increase due to fluoxetine treatment. → 50%, The number of patients with body dysmorphic disorder that needs treatment to achieve one case of improvement. → 2, The rate of improvement when taking fluoxetine. → 3/4


explanation:
Step1: Draw a 2X2 table

Improved at 6 months Not improved at 6 months

Fluoxetine 75 ?25 100

Placebo 25 ?75 100

100 100 200

Step 2: Calculate event rates: Here 'event' is 'getting improved.' CER: 25/100 (chance that a subject on placebo will improve) EER: 75/100 (= 3/4 - the rate of improvement when taking fluoxetine) Step 3: Calculate RR RR = EER/CER = 75/25 = 3 Step 4: Calculate OR OR = cross product = 75X75 / 25X25 = 9 (The odds of getting better while taking fluoxetine compared to placebo for 6 months) Step 5: ARR or BI = CER-EER = 50/100 = 50% (The absolute benefit increase due to fluoxetine treatment) Step 6: NNT = 1/ARR = 100/50 = 2 (The number of patients with body dysmorphic disorder that needs treatment to achieve one case of improvement)

The relative risk of developing psychosis for cannabis smokers compared with non-smokers Choose...

The percentage of psychosis that can be attributed to smoking cannabis Choose...

correctAnswer: The relative risk of developing psychosis for cannabis smokers compared with non-smokers → 8, The percentage of psychosis that can be attributed to smoking cannabis → 87.5%, The excess incidence rate of psychosis that could be averted in the community if cannabis smoking is reduced to 5% → 3.5/100,000
explanation: Explanations: Step 1: Relative risk = incidence rate in exposed / incidence rate in nonexposed. (We can also express this as RR = EER/CER. Here incidence rates are given which represent risk or event rates.) RR = 80/10 = 8  Step 2: The percentage of psychosis that can be attributed to smoking cannabis is Attributable risk proportion: = AR/ EER (or differences in incidence / incidence in the exposed) = (80-10) X 100 / 80 = 87.5% Step 3: If the prevalence of smoking was reduced to 5%, the population attributable risk (PAR) = attributable risk x prevalence of exposure in the population =70/100,000 × 5/100 = 3.5/100,000.

NNT = 1/ARR. 3) Absolute risk reduction is the difference in risk between the control and experimental group. ARR=CER-EER 4) Experimental Event Rate (EER) is the rate of an event (e.g. improvement, side effect, etc.,) in the experimental group. correctAnswer:
The ability of a test to correctly identify true positives among the ill subjects → Sensitivity, The ability of a test to correctly identify true negatives among the healthy subjects → Specificity, The proportion who are ill among all subjects who are picked up by a test as having the disorder → Positive predictive value, The proportion who are truly well among all subjects who are declared to be well by a test → Negative predictive value, This helps to determine how the result of a diagnostic test influences the probability that the patient has the disorder. → Likelihood ratio

explanation:
 Sensitivity is the proportion of the 'diseased subjects', who are picked up by the test as having the disorder. In other words, it is the ability of the test to identify those who really have the disorder. Specificity is the proportion of 'well subjects', who are excluded by the test as not having the disorder. In other words, it is the ability of the test to identify those who really do not have the disorder. Positive predictive value (PPV) is defined as the proportion of positive test results for which disease is confirmed. In other words, it is the proportion of the test positives who are true positives. Negative predictive value (NPV) is the proportion of negative test results for which a disease is absent. In other words, it is the proportion of the test negatives who are true negatives.

Likelihood ratio summarises how many times more (or less) likely patients with the disease are to have that particular result than patients without the disease. It is the ratio of the probability of the specific test result in people who do have the disease to the probability in people who do not.

An open cohort of patients registered with these practices during the 10-year study period (January 1, 1995, to July 1, 2005) was included. The sample consisted of 40 441 incident cases of 6 cancers (breast, colon, rectal, gastroesophageal, prostate, and respiratory). Odds ratios were computed for cancer risk association with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, after adjusting for smoking, body mass index, socioeconomic status, comorbidities, and prescribed medications, including antipsychotics. Patients with bipolar disorder had cancer risks similar to patients with neither condition after adjustment. APGAR scores for asphyxia were assigned by a midwife using the birth records, and confirmed by 2 paediatricians independently with excellent agreement between the two raters (? 0.83). In addition, the presence or absence of pre- eclampsia was also recorded in accordance with a predefined criteria. Other indicators of foetal growth impairment such as low birth weight, delay (>7 days) in gaining weight after birth, birth length and head circumference were also recorded. Indicators of hypoxia/ischaemia around birth such as emergency Caesarean section, placental abruption, cord prolapse, foetal heart rate <100 or >160 b.p.m., and prolonged hospital stay for the child were also noted. Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for schizophrenia in relation to individual obstetric complications were calculated for matched case--control sets using conditional logistic regression. Odds ratios were adjusted for possible confounding variables, both one by one and simultaneously. Results: The results are shown in the below table. Adjusting either separately or simultaneously for maternal history of psychotic illness, maternal age, parity, socio-economic classification, civil status and attendance at antenatal care did not substantially alter the odds ratios for most of the obstetric complications listed. However, after adjusting for these possible confounding variables, the odds ratio for schizophrenia in relation to signs of asphyxia at  birth was increased to 4.5 (95% CI 2.2-9.5). The authors estimated a population-attributable fraction for birth asphyxia as 7.7% for schizophrenia using the data for population prevalence of birth asphyxia in Stockholm (not discussed in the study). Comparatively uncommon exposures such as pre-eclampsia, low birth-weight and short gestational age (<33 weeks) showed increased risk estimates but were not statistically significant. stem: Which of the following describes 'diagnostic accuracy' of a screening test?
options: Proportion of screened sample that is correctly classified by the screening test
Proportion of screened sample with the disease
Proportion of diseased sample classified correctly by the screening test
Proportion of positively tested sample with the disease                                                                                    
Proportion of non-diseased sample classified correctly by the screening test
correctAnswer: Proportion of screened sample that is correctly classified by the screening test
explanation: The term 'diagnostic accuracy' is not often used. It is replaced by much finer measures of sensitivity and specificity. Accuracy is given by all correct hits / total number of observations.

stem: Two diagnostic tests are carried out in tandem. Those who test positive for the first test are further tested using the second test in a serial manner. If the two tests are considered as a single diagnostic battery for final results, which of the following is correct?
options: The sensitivity and specificity are unchanged
The sensitivity and specificity depends on the order of individual test application
The battery has higher sensitivity than the individual tests
The battery has higher specificity than individual tests
The battery has lower sensitivity and specificity than individual tests
correctAnswer: The battery has higher specificity than individual tests
explanation: When two sequential tests are used, and those who test positive by the first test are brought in for the second test, there is a net loss in sensitivity, but a net gain in specificity, compared with either test alone. However, when two simultaneous tests are used, there is a net gain in sensitivity and a net loss of specificity, compared with either test alone. 

explanation: The likelihood ratio of a positive test (LR+) is the ratio of the likelihood (probability) of a positive test result in the population with disease divided by the likelihood of a positive test result in the population without disease. stem: A pilot project carried out by DVLA uses a weekly cut-off of 21 units to define alcohol misuse. If this cut-off is reduced to 14 units which of the following might happen?
explanation: The dilemma involved in deciding whether to set a high cutoff or a low cutoff rests in the problem of the false positives and the false  negatives that result from the testing. explanation: Every one of us, after getting results of a test for a patient, want to know only one thing - "Given this test result, what is the likelihood that the patient has the disease?" Sensitivity and specificity are characteristics of the test - not of the patient with a particular test result. The  most useful measure to answer the above is the predictive value. This is affected by two factors: the prevalence of the disease in the population tested and, if the disease is rare, the specificity of the test being used. For a negative test result, the Negative predictive value will be more useful.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents with cognitive difficulties and has a score of 24 in MMSE. It is reported that MMSE scores = 25 has a sensitivity of 80% and specificity of 90% to detect dementia. explanation: To determine the posttest probability, we must first determine the post-test odds. Post-test odds are given by LR X pretest odds. Pretest odds can be calculated from the prevalence which is, in fact, the pretest probability. Here likelihood ratio for positive test is given by LR+ =  sensitivity / (1-specificity) = 8. Posttest odds = 1/9 X 8 = 8/9. Post-test probability = 8/17 = 0.47

Assuming that urine dip-test for pregnancy has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 88% what is the probability that your patient, if pregnant, will have two consecutive negative pregnancy tests?
explanation:  Assuming the two test results to be independent of each other, we can multiply the probability of a negative test result in 'truly diseased' to achieve the probability at the end of consecutive negative tests. The probability of a negative test if there is pregnancy is given by false negative rate = (Test negative)/ (disease positive). This can be obtained from 1-sensitivity. Here it is (1 - 0.9 =0.1). stem: The Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale (WEMWBS) was developed to meet the demand for instruments to measure mental well- being. It comprises 14 positively phrased Likert-style items and fulfils classic criteria for scale development. The authors report the internal construct validity of WEMWBS from the perspective of the Rasch measurement model. The model was applied to data collected from 779 respondents (aged 16 –74 (average 41.9) yrs) in Wave 12 (Autumn 2006) of the Scottish Health Education Population Survey. Initial fit to model expectations was poor. The items 'I've been feeling good about myself', 'I've been interested in new things' and 'I've been feeling cheerful' all showed significant misfit to model expectations and were deleted. This led to a marginal improvement in fit to the model. After further analysis, more items were deleted, and a strict unidimensional seven-item scale (the Short Warwick Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale (SWEMWBS)) was resolved. Many items deleted because of misfit with model expectations showed considerable bias for gender. Two retained items also demonstrated a bias for gender but, at the scale level, cancelled out. One further retained item 'I've been feeling optimistic about the future' showed bias for age. The correlation between the 14 item and 7 item versions was 0.954. The authors concluded that the short 7-item version of WEMWBS was found to satisfy the strict unidimensionality expectations of the Rasch model, and be largely free of bias. This scale, SWEMWBS, provides a raw score-interval scale transformation for use in parametric procedures. In terms of face validity, SWEMWBS presents a more restricted view of mental well-being than the 14 item WEMWBS, with most items representing aspects of psychological and eudemonic well-being, and few covering hedonic well-being or affect. However, robust measurement properties combined with brevity make SWEMWBS preferable to WEMWBS at present for monitoring mental well-being in populations. Where face validity is an issue, the authors favour continuing to collect data on the full 14 item WEMWBS. Stewart-Brown et al., Health and Quality of Life Outcomes 2009, 7:15. stem: A meta-analysis summarises ten studies and reports a significant Cochran Q test result. Which of the following is the correct interpretation
options: Significant homogeneity exists among the reported studies
Methodological quality of individual studies are significantly inferior to summary results
The summary estimate is statistically significant

correctAnswer: Significant heterogeneity exists among the reported studies
explanation: Cochran's Q test is the traditional test for heterogeneity. It tests the null hypothesis that all of the apparent variability is due to chance (i.e. no statistical heterogeneity is present). The test is in a way a modified test of ?two probability distribution; if the test generates a low p-value it means the null hypothesis is rejected i.e. statistical heterogeneity exists. If the p-value is low (say, less than 0.1) investigators should look for possible explanations including differences in patients profile, interventions, measurement of outcomes and study design. If the p-value  gets very low (less than 0.01) one must avoid or reconsider the use of pooled single best estimates of treatment effects. But this test is sensitive to the sample size of individual studies - when studies have included only a few patients it may be difficult to reject the null hypothesis even if it is false. On the other hand, when sample sizes are very large, even small differences in effect size that may not be clinically meaningful, may nevertheless generate low p-values.

stem: Which of the following is the most important assumption made when choosing fixed effect analysis in a systematic review

No difference is noted between the outcome of individual studies
Difference in outcome of individual studies is due to different scales used
Difference in outcome of individual studies is due to chance
Difference in outcome of individual studies is due to variations between studies
correctAnswer: Difference in outcome of individual studies is due to chance
explanation: The usual method of meta-analysis assumes that all the studies are estimating the same effect and only random variation between research subjects within a study leads the observed study effects to vary. We call this the fixed effects model. Here we assume that the effect to be estimated is the same in all studies and use only the sampling variation within the studies. In other words, we assume that any difference between studies is due to chance. When one cannot explain why different studies exploring the same phenomenon throw up different  results and estimates, we can use the random effects model to arrive at pooled estimate. We estimate both the variability between subjects within the studies (consider this to be equivalent to sampling variation) and the variation between studies (population variability). In such circumstances, the result of each  individual study can be standardized by calculating a standardized mean difference (SMD) which is the difference of the means of both treatment arms divided by the pooled standard deviation. explanation: Results from trials that have measured the same outcome on the same scale can readily be combined in a meta-analysis by calculating the weighted mean difference. To quantitatively examine the literature to date reporting the transition risk to psychosis in subjects at clinical high risk, electronic databases were searched until January 2011 and all studies reporting transition risks in patients at clinical high risk were retrieved. The High-Risk state was defined using either the Ultra High-Risk criteria (MELBOURNE) or the Basic Symptoms criteria (BONN) using instruments such as the CAARMS, the Basel Screening Instrument for Psychosis and SIPS. Across the overall database, the pooled mean transition risk to a full psychotic episode from an HR state was 29.2% (95% CI, 27.3%-31.1%), with a mean follow-up of 31 months. This risk was independent of the psychometric instruments used and was estimated to be 18% after 6 months of follow-up, 22% after 1 year, 29% after 2 years, and 36% after 3 years. To provide a visual representation of the time course, a subset of studies (n = 6) with necessary data are summarized in the below Figure. (Fusar-Poli et al.. stem: Which one among the following is essentially an observational study of the evidence that allows large quantities of information to be speedily refined and reduced to a manageable size?
explanation: A systematic review is essentially an observational study of the evidence that allows large quantities of information to be speedily refined and reduced to a manageable size. It is a scientific evaluation of several studies that have been conducted on a specific clinical question. By pooling together, the evidence drawn from systematic reviews can be very powerful and influential indeed. (Ref: Making sense of critical  appraisal: Ajetunmobi- Pg 154)

stem: Which one among the following is not a procedure followed when conducting a systematic review?
explanation: The typical stages in a systematic overview include 1) specification of evidence sought 2) identification of evidence 3) critical appraisal of evidence 4) synthesis of evidence (Higgins 2008). Randomisation is not a step involved in this process.

stem: Which of the following statements is inaccurate about risk ratios in meta-analytical studies?
options: Risk ratio is calculated by dividing the risk in the treated group by the risk in the control group
Risk ratio of less than 1 indicates no difference between the groups
Risk ratios are frequently given with their confidence intervals
Risk ratios are used to investigate the effects of a treatment
If the confidence interval does not contain 1, it is statistically significant
correctAnswer: Risk ratio of less than 1 indicates no difference between the groups
explanation: Risk ratios are used to investigate the effects of a treatment. The risk ratio is calculated by dividing the risk in the treated group by the risk in the control group. A risk ratio of 1 indicates no difference between the groups. Risk ratios are frequently given with their confidence intervals. If the confidence interval does not contain 1 (no difference in risk), it is statistically significant. 

stem: Which of the following statements is inaccurate regarding search strategy for systematic reviews?
options: Searching one electronic database is insufficient
It is important to focus on peer-reviewed published studies
It is important to search for studies in all languages, not just English
The search strategy used needs to be exhaustive
The search strategy must be comprehensive
correctAnswer: It is important to focus on peer-reviewed published studies 
explanation: It is important to search for both published and unpublished studies, in all languages, not just English. The search strategy used needs to be comprehensive and exhaustive using different electronic databases. All these measures could help to avoid publication bias.

stem: Which one among the following is not essential for conducting a meta-analysis?
options: Recording of data from the individual studies
Establishing criteria for including and excluding studies
Researcher being an expert in the field of inquiry
correctAnswer: Researcher being an expert in the field of inquiry 
explanation: The four basic steps for conducting a meta-analysis include (1) Literature search, (2) Establishing criteria for including and excluding studies (3) Recording of data from the individual studies, and (4) Statistical analysis of the data.

stem: Which plot can be used to detect publication bias?
explanation: Publication bias can be detected by constructing a funnel plot of all identifiable studies that have been performed on a clinical subject. A funnel plot involves plotting the study size against the odds ratio. Any biases in reporting will skew the normally symmetrical shape of the plot. 

stem: While conducting a systematic review, publication bias could be determined using all of the following methods except
options: Confidence interval of the pooled effect size
Soliciting and comparing published vs. unpublished data
correctAnswer:
Confidence interval of the pooled effect size 

explanation: Publication bias can be detected using all of the various listed methods except using the confidence interval of the pooled estimate. The confidence interval of the pooled estimate is a function of the total sample size and the number of trials included in a meta-analysis.

stem: Two hospitals in Nottinghamshire are managed by the same NHS trust. The managers note that the duration of hospital admission in the inpatient units to be significantly different between them affecting the bed occupancy rates unfavourably in one area. If the managers intend to compare the length of stay in these two hospitals, which of the following methods is preferable?
options: Chi square test of 'long' admissions in each hospital
Analysis of variance of admission duration
F test of mean admission duration
explanation: Survival methods are best suited to measuring "time to an event" i.e. discharge from hospital. These methods do not require a near-normal distribution of values; such parametric assumptions are needed for a t-test or F-test (ANOVA). The chi-square test, in this case, would involve loss of significant information due to dichotomisation of the data.

stem: In survival analysis using Kaplan-Meier method, which of the following is plotted on the y axis?
options: Time remaining after achieving an outcome
Proportion of those who achieved the outcome of interest
Proportion of those who have not achieved the outcome of interest
Life expectancy at each point of observation
Time taken for achieving an outcome
correctAnswer: Proportion of those who have not achieved the outcome of interest
explanation: In analyzing survival data, two functions that are dependent on time are of particular interest: the survival function and the hazard function. The survival function S(t) is defined as the probability of surviving at least to time t. The hazard function h(t) is the conditional probability of dying at time t having survived to that time. The graph of S(t) against t is called the survival curve (Retrieved from http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1065034/). The Kaplan-Meier method can be used to estimate this curve wherein S(t) is given  by proportion of individuals surviving an anticipated outcome - this is plotted along the y-axis while time period is plotted across the x-axis. Note that survival curves are sometimes plotted with a logarithmic vertical scale, making the survival curves look like straight lines. This may be misleading if one does not attend to the plots expressed.

stem: Which of the following is the most important outcome of interest in survival analysis?
options: Cost of setting up a service
Number of cases surviving an intervention
Time taken to achieve an event of interest
Mean score achieved by two groups at the outcome
correctAnswer: Time taken to achieve an event of interest 
explanation: The probability of surviving a condition for a given duration is the most important parameter of interest for survival curves. This can also yield time taken to achieve an event of interest in individuals belonging to the observed cohort.

stem: Which of the following tests can be applied if you want to test if smokers differ significantly from non-smokers with respect to risk of depression over the 10 year period, irrespective of other systematic differences between the two groups?
explanation: The log-rank test enables us to assess the influence of a categorical variable on survival.

stem: Which of the following tests can be applied if you want to test if smokers differ significantly from non-smokers with respect to risk of depression over the 10 year period after adjusting for the confounding effect of age and alcohol intake?
explanation: The log-rank test enables us to assess the influence of a categorical variable on survival. But if we want to assess the influence of a continuous variable, such as age, weight, or blood pressure, we need proportional hazards (or Cox) regression (Excerpt retrieved from https://www.med.illinois.edu/m2/epidemiology/tahandouts/survival). This method allows us to consider several variables simultaneously.  Thus, we can produce estimates of the effect of each variable, adjusting for the others. This can help us distinguish between a variable that has an independent effect on survival, and one whose effect on survival is due only to its association with another variable

stem: Which of the following assumptions must be met before applying Cox's proportional hazard test?
options: The survival curves cross each other during the period of follow-up
The median survival time is reached during the period of follow-up
The hazard ratio is constant over time
At least 50% of the observed events must have occurred in the first year of observation
Confounders have no effect on survival time
correctAnswer:
The hazard ratio is constant over time

 

© 2023 SPMM Course Limited, UK. Refund Policy | Terms & Conditions


explanation: We can use either log-rank test or Cox test to determine statistically the difference between two survival curves. The log-rank test is used to test whether there is a difference between the survival times of different groups, but it does not allow other explanatory variables to be taken into account. Cox's proportional hazards model is analogous to a multiple regression models and enables the difference between survival times of particular groups of patients to be tested while allowing for other factors. In this model, the response (dependent) variable  is the 'hazard'. The hazard is the probability of dying (or experiencing the event in question) given that patients have survived up to a given point in time, or the risk for death at that moment. In Cox's model no assumption is made about the probability distribution of the hazard (Retrieved from http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1065034/). However, it is assumed that the ratio of the risk for dying at a particular point in time between one group and the other is constant all the time. In other words, Cox test assumes that the hazard ratio does not depend on time.

stem: A CPD programme for mental health practitioners is aimed at improving communication skills. A quiz is administered prior to the start of the programme and again following the completion. The practitioners attending the programme are at the 4th percentile of quiz score at pretest. At posttest, they are around the 20th percentile. Apart from concluding that the programme is very effective which of the following could explain the change in scores
explanation: Repeatedly measuring the participants may lead to bias. Participants may remember the correct answers or may be conditioned to know  that they are being tested. Repeatedly taking (the same or similar) verbal performance tests usually leads to scoring gains - beware of being falsely reassured when taking the same mock exam before and after a one-day course!

stem: Patients in the control groups of randomized clinical trials seem to have a better clinical course than similar patients who do not participate in trials. All of the following may contribute to this trial participation effect except
options: Use of higher potency of medications
Selection criteria for clinical trials may screen out the sickest patients
Frequent monitoring and extra clinical care
More experienced clinicians and academic centres
correctAnswer: Use of higher potency of medications
explanation: It is more likely that participation in clinical trials by itself (irrespective of the intervention received) has a positive effect on the outcome of patients.The suggested reasons include better clinical input with experienced research-clinicians, better treatments, favourable selection criteria, the placebo effect (or participation effect) and better use of treatment protocols. BMJ 2005;330:1164 (21 May) 

stem: Which one of the following would not be expected to increase the statistical power of a clinical trial to test a new medical treatment
options: Lengthening the trial to allow enrollment of more patients
Adopting stronger measures to ensure compliance with therapy
Treating a more clinically homogeneous group of patients
Adopting a more stringent standard of evidence to prove the new treatment works
Testing only a subgroup of patients for whom the new drug would be expected to have the greatest advantage
correctAnswer: Adopting a more stringent standard of evidence to prove the new treatment works
explanation: The general formula for calculating a test statistic is test statistic = (x - µ) / (s /vN) where x = the sample estimate, µ = the hypothesized value, and s /vN the standard error of x. Power (ability to detect true difference if it exists) would be affected by the effect size being tested (x - µ), the sample size (n), and the variability (standard deviation) among the samples (s). Adopting a more stringent standard of evidence means it will be difficult to demonstrate significance in smaller samples - one will require larger sample size to generate the required power. Enrolling  more patients, testing a subgroup with a higher probability of hypothesised outcome or a more homogeneous group (i.e. lower variability) and ensuring adherence (low dropouts, low missing data), etc. can increase the power.

stem: A drug firm reanalysed its data submitted for licensing an antidepressant ten years ago. The analysis indicated that the Number needed to harm NNH for the suicidal act when using the antidepressant was 60. The original data included 500 subjects in placebo arm out of which 50 exhibited suicidal acts. There were 600 subjects in the active antidepressant arm. Calculate the number of subjects in the active arm that exhibited suicidal acts
explanation:
Calculating NNH needs calculation of ARR (Absolute risk reduction). As NNH for antidepressants is 60, this means the event rate must be  higher for antidepressants than placebo. In other words, the risk of a side effect is likely to be lower with placebo. ARR = experimental event rate - control event rate (i.e., EER-CER) NNH = 1/ARR. ARR = 1/NNH = 1/60 for this study. Control event rate is given as 50/500. We are asked to calculate no. of experimental events. This can be derived from experimental event rate. So here ARR = (EER - (50/500)). Replacing known values, 1/60 = ((no. of experimental events/600)-(1/10)) No. of experimental events/600 = (1/60)+(1/10) No. of experimental events/600 = (1/60)+(6/60) = (7/60)

No. of experimental events = (1/60)+(6/60) = (7/60) * 600 = 7*10 = 70

stem: In a study comparing drug A and placebo control, 20 out of 200 patients taking drug A die after three years. 25 out of 225 patients taking the placebo die after three years. If death is the outcome of interest, the number of patients who need to take drug A to prevent one death is
explanation: In this case ARR = 1/90. Hence, NNT will be 90. Guyatt G Rennie D et al. Users' guide to the medical literature: JAMA evidence 2nd ed. McGrawHill 2008. Pg 82

stem: Which of the following statements regarding non-adherence and intention to treat analysis in RCTs is true
options: Intention-to-treat analysis distorts the principle of randomisation
The prognostic factors are comparable between adherent and non-adherent subjects
Subjects randomised to placebo arm but did not adhere to prescription have better prognosis than those who adhere to placebo.
A subject who dies before receiving the first dose of placebo must be excluded from intention-to-treat analysis
A subject who gets 'cured' before completing the trial must be included in intention-to-treat analysis
correctAnswer: A subject who gets 'cured' before completing the trial must be included in intention-to-treat analysis
explanation: Removing patients after randomization always risks introducing bias by creating noncomparable groups. Hence, Intention to treat analyses must include those who are randomised but not received the intended intervention in the final analysis. Guyatt G Rennie D et al. Users' guide to the medical literature: JAMA evidence 2nd ed. McGrawHill 2008. Pg 173 

stem: A study reports that 20% of a control group had a relapse of schizophrenia during the trial period, while only 15% of the treatment group relapsed. Which of the following is a valid statement based on the above information
options: The treatment is 15% effective in reducing the relapse
The outcome has been treated as a dichotomous variable
The relative risk of relapse in treatment group compared to controls will be >1
The treatment can prevent 20% of relapses
The treatment reduces the risk of death by 5%
correctAnswer: The outcome has been treated as a dichotomous variable
explanation: As the results are in proportion, one can conclude safely that the variable was dichotomous. The numbers 15% and 20% are event rates - they are not risk reduction rates.Guyatt G Rennie D et al. Users' guide to the medical literature: JAMA evidence 1st ed. McGrawHill 2002 Pg66 

stem: To be statistically significant, the confidence intervals of relative risk reduction achieved by an intervention should not cross
explanation: The value for a statistic corresponding to no effect in the population is called the null value. For correlations, risk difference, relative risk reduction (RRR) and changes in the mean, the null value is zero. If the outcome statistic is a relative risk or odds ratio, the null value is 1 (equal risk or odds). So for RRR the result is statistically significant if the confidence interval does not overlap zero. 

stem: An article reporting a trial does not provide confidence intervals around the point estimate of relative risk. If the p-value achieved by the treatment effect is exactly p=0.05, then the lower bound of the 95% confidence limit for the relative risk is likely to be
explanation: For a statistically non-significant result (i.e. p-value more than 0.05) the lower confidence limit of RR might have been less than 1. As the p- value is exactly 0.05, the lower confidence limit of RR is likely to be one. 

stem: 95% CI for the relative risk reduction achieved by an intervention in an expensive multicentre RCT is -28% to 49%; Which of the following conclusions can be valid
options: 28% of patients will show a negative effect
More people who take the intervention will have positive response than negative response
The RCT really has not helped to decide whether or not to offer the new treatment
95% of patients will have treatment response between -28% and 49%
The maximum benefit that can be achieved by the drug is 49%.
correctAnswer: The RCT really has not helped to decide whether or not to offer the new treatment
explanation: These results are consistent with both an RRR of -28% (that is, patients given the new treatment might be 28% more likely to die than control patients) and an RRR of nearly 49% (that is, patients subsequently receiving the new treatment might have a risk of dying almost 50% less than those who are not treated). In other words, the 95% CI on this RRR is -28% to 49%, and the trial really has not helped us decide whether  or not to offer the new treatment.Guyatt G Rennie D et al. Users' guide to the medical literature: JAMA evidence 2nd ed. McGrawHill 2008 Pg 77

stem: A trial randomized 100 patients each to treatment and control groups; there were 20 relapses in the control group and 15 relapses in the treatment group. What will happen to the point estimate of relative risk reduction if the sample size is increased to 1000 a group, but the event rates remain stable
options: The point estimate is more likely to cross the zero value
The 95% confidence intervals around the estimate become less precise
The point estimate moves farther away from the true population value
Point estimate of RRR stays the same
The upper bound of the 95% limits is most likely to be in negative values
correctAnswer: Point estimate of RRR stays the same
explanation: As RR is EER/CER, it will not change by merely increasing sample size but having same event rate (though this may be nearly impossible practically). As RR does not change, RR (which is 1 - RR) may not change. Guyatt G Rennie D et al. Users' guide to the medical literature: JAMA  evidence 2nd ed. McGrawHill 2008Pg78

stem: A group therapist leading a smoking cessation group becomes curious about the effectiveness of new drug varenicline on smoking cessation. She approaches an interested pharmacist, and together they recruit 60 smokers attending the group. She asks for volunteers to undergo the drug trial. 30 volunteers are given varenicline for 12 weeks. At the end of 12 weeks 'frequency of smoking urges' is compared using a validated scale. Which of the following components of a drug evaluation trial is missing in this experiment
explanation: Lack of randomisation is a serious threat to the external validity of intervention trials. A sample may have certain features that may interact  with the independent variable, limiting generalizability. Note that the inferences here are based on volunteers in a smoking cessation group. It is likely that non-volunteers have a poor motivation and may respond in a significantly different fashion to what is demonstrated by this study - randomised sampling would have helped in generalisation of the results.

stem: Which of the following conditions encourage acceptance of a result from subgroup analysis in an RCT
options: Primary hypothesis is not proven but subgroup analysis shows a significant result
Multiple subgroups are analysed but only one showed a clear statistical significance
The subgroup hypothesis was specified before the study began
Other studies fail to replicate the subgroup findings
The effect size for subgroup falls within the 95% confidence limits of the primary outcome
correctAnswer: The subgroup hypothesis was specified before the study began
explanation: Most proponents of EBM advise us to remain skeptical of subgroup analyses. A treatment is likely to benefit the subgroup more or less than the other patients only if the difference in the effects of treatment in the subgroups is large and very unlikely to occur by chance. Even when these conditions apply, the results may be misleading if investigators did not specify their hypotheses before the study began, if they had a very large number of hypotheses, or if other studies fail to replicate the finding. Guyatt G Rennie D et al. Users' guide to the medical  literature: JAMA evidence 2nd ed. McGrawHill 2008 Pg80

stem: Which of the following is NOT a surrogate or substitute endpoint for a treatment trial
options: Working memory scores in donepezil trials for schizophrenia patients with negative syndrome
Impulsivity score in atomoxetine trials for ADHD
Activities of daily living scores in dementia trials
Lipid levels in a trial of statins for antipsychotic-related metabolic syndrome
Glycosylated haemoglobin levels when using rosiglitazone for patients with clozapine induced diabetes.
correctAnswer: Activities of daily living scores in dementia trials
explanation: Surrogate outcomes are often attractive for reducing sample size and decreasing the length of follow-up and sometimes even enabling ethical approval of studies. Unfortunately, they can be misleading. Any outcome that is easily measurable but used as a proxy for the actual primary outcome of direct benefit to patients is a surrogate outcome. Guyatt G Rennie D et al. Users' guide to the medical literature: JAMA evidence 2nd ed. McGrawHill 2008 Pg81 

stem: In a patient with many risk factors for metabolic syndrome and taking risperidone for schizophrenia, the 3-year risk of stroke is estimated to be 30%. If he takes co-prescribed statins during this period, this risk drops to 20%. What is the NNT to prevent stroke in this patient
explanation: ARR = 10%. Hence NNT = 100/10 = 10.

stem: Which of the following is true concerning the interpretation of a randomised trial results
options: Relative risk reduction is the same as risk difference
Relative risk is obtained by subtracting 1 from odds ratio
Odds ratio must never be equated to relative risk in RCTs
Relative risk is generally far higher that risk difference (ARR)
If the event rates are very high odds ratio may be equivalent to relative risk
correctAnswer: Relative risk is generally far higher that risk difference (ARR)
explanation: Failing to distinguish between the OR and the RR when interpreting randomized trial results will seldom mislead us. However, we must correctly distinguish between the RR and the RD (risk difference or ARR). This is because the RR is generally far larger than the RD, and presentations of results in the form of RR (or RRR) can convey a misleading message. For example, reducing a patient's risk by 50% sounds impressive. That may, however, represent a reduction in risk from 2% to 1%. The corresponding 1% ARR sounds considerably less  impressive. Guyatt G Rennie D et al. Users' guide to the medical literature: JAMA evidence 2nd ed. McGrawHill 2008. Pg90

stem: Which of the following is correct concerning NNT to prevent an event of relapse in a treatment trial
options: NNT is inversely proportional to the baseline relapse rate
NNT is directly proportional to the relative risk reduction
For a given population, a more effective treatment with twice the RRR will double the NNT
If the risk of relapse in your clinical population is two times higher, you have to treat twice the number of patients to prevent one
If the same treatment is applied to a different population with half the relapse rate, the NNT halves.
correctAnswer: NNT is inversely proportional to the baseline relapse rate
explanation: Assuming a constant RRR, the NNT is inversely related to the proportion of patients in the control group who have an adverse event (CER). If the risk of an adverse event doubles (for example, if we deal with patients at a higher risk of depression than those included in the clinical trial of antidepressants), we need to treat only half as many patients to prevent an adverse event; if the risk decreases by a factor of 4  (patients are younger, have less comorbidity than those in the study), we will have to treat 4 times as many people. The NNT is also inversely related to the RRR. With the same baseline risk, a more effective treatment with twice the RRR will reduce the NNT by half. If the RRR with one treatment is only a quarter of that achieved by an alternative strategy, the NNT will be four times greater. Guyatt G Rennie D et al. Users' guide to the medical literature: JAMA evidence 2nd ed. McGrawHill 2008. Pg90

stem: An investigator is interested not only in the total number of new-onset hyperlipidaemia following antipsychotic use, but also in the timing of onset after initiating the treatment. So he attempts to calculate an average measure of the relative risk weighted for number of patients at risk over a long period of follow-up in the trial cohort. This measure is best described as
explanation: The weighted RR over the entire study in a survival analysis is known as the hazard ratio. 

stem: Which of the following cannot be identified from confidence intervals of an outcome measure such as relative risk in a treatment trial
options: The range within which the true treatment effect is likely to lie
The degree of certainty attached to a range of values within which the true effect lies
The statistical significance of a trial result
The precision of a trial result
The proportion of patients in the population who will have the estimated value of outcome
correctAnswer: The proportion of patients in the population who will have the estimated value of outcome
explanation: The range within which the effect is likely to lie can be given by confidence intervals of a point estimate. Precision and degree of certainty can be given by confidence limits. One can understand statistical significance using p-values. The proportion of patients in the population who will have the estimated value of outcome cannot be determined from a trial estimate of RR 

stem: Which of the following is an appropriate way of interpreting negative trial results?
options: NNT is called NNH if the point estimate fails to reach preset level of statistical significance
If the upper bound of confidence intervals contain an important treatment benefit, a beneficial effect cannot be ruled out
If the confidence intervals cross point of no effect, the treatment is conclusively useless
If the p value of point estimate is >0.05, the treatment is harmful
If the p value of point estimate is >0.05, the treatment offers no benefit
correctAnswer: If the upper bound of confidence intervals contain an important treatment benefit, a beneficial effect cannot be ruled out
explanation: An apparently negative trial generally has a P value greater than 0.05; so it fails to exclude the null hypothesis that treatment and control interventions do not differ). In this case, one can focus on the upper bound of the confidence interval (that is, the end that suggests the largest benefit from treatment). If this value excludes any important benefit of treatment, we can conclude that the trial is definitively negative. But if the confidence interval includes an important benefit, the possibility that the treatment still might be worthwhile must not be  ruled out. Guyatt G Rennie D et al. Users' guide to the medical literature: JAMA evidence 2nd ed. McGrawHill 2008. Pg 104

stem: Which of the following comments regarding validity and reliability of research studies is correct
options: Random errors affect validity more than reliability
Biased studies produce valid results which are unreliable
Smaller samples yield results with less validity
Large sample size reduces the likelihood of bias
Random errors have more influence on the results of smaller studies
correctAnswer: Random errors have more influence on the results of smaller studies
explanation: In a study with large sample size, random errors become less prominent while in studies of smaller sample size the likelihood of a misleading result through random error is high. But note that bias (a threat to validity) does not disappear by merely increasing sample size. Biased studies can produce results that can be reproduced, but still not true. While random errors affect reliability more, bias affects validity to a higher degree. Guyatt G Rennie D et al. Users' guide to the medical literature: JAMA evidence 2nd ed. McGrawHill 2008. Pg 112 

stem: Choose one correct statement with respect to randomised trials that are stopped early
options: Perceived harm due to the intervention does not warrant early cessation
RCTs that are stopped early yield more data on safety and toxicity
Early cessation is unethical under all circumstances
The most common reason for premature cessation is early appearance of a large treatment effect
Early cessation of RCTs generally underestimates the treatment effect
correctAnswer: The most common reason for premature cessation is early appearance of a large treatment effect
explanation: Investigators may stop randomized controlled trials (RCTs) earlier than planned because of perceived harm of the experimental intervention, because they lose hope in achieving a positive result, or because the sponsor wishes to save money. The most common reason for early stopping, however, is that investigators note treatment effects that appear to be unlikely by chance (and that are often large) and that persuade them that the experimental intervention is beneficial. Guyatt G Rennie D et al. Users' guide to the medical literature: JAMA  evidence 2nd ed. McGrawHill 2008. Pg 161

stem: Which of the following types of RCT is not subject to confounding by age, sex, or other individual variables obviating the need for examination of distribution of baseline characteristics following randomisation
options: RCT with three arms of comparison
explanation: Crossover clinical trials are not subject to confounding by age, sex, or most personal characteristics. But they are not useful in studies using irreversible endpoints such as 'complete cure' from a disease or death event. They need fewer people than parallel group trials as each individual plays the part of a 'trial subject' twice. 

stem: In which of the following circumstances is an n-of-1 trial most suitable
options: To compare the effectiveness of two different interventions for a self limiting condition and open cholecystectomy in female patients
Presence of RCTs demonstrating some beneficial effect for the intervention in study samples
To evaluate treatment response for a patient with an acute and rapidly evolving illness
To evaluate the effectiveness of a medication in preventing stroke
To compare laparascopic and open cholecystectomy in female patients
correctAnswer: Presence of RCTs demonstrating some beneficial effect for the intervention in study samples
explanation: N of 1 trials are most useful when one or several RCTs may have shown that the treatment in question is highly effective but 50% or more of patients in such trials have proved unresponsive, leaving the question whether our patient will respond or not. No useful result can be achieved if one attempts to experiment with a completely unknown intervention in n-of-1 fashion. For self-limiting conditions, preventive interventions, in rapidly changing illnesses and for irreversible treatments, n of 1 model may not be suitable. Guyatt G Rennie D et al. Users'  guide to the medical literature: JAMA evidence 2nd ed. McGrawHill 2008. Pg 183

stem: In which of the following circumstances an n-of-1 trial is not recommended
options: The patient and clinician differ in their opinion regarding the usefulness of a certain drug which the patients insists to prescribe
To find the optimal dose of a medication the patient should receive.
To evaluate a treatment that has potentially curative effect on a longstanding condition though evidence is weak
The patient has been started on a medication that has inconclusive evidence with regard to beneficial effect
A patient has symptoms that are suspected to be an adverse effect
correctAnswer: To evaluate a treatment that has potentially curative effect on a longstanding condition though evidence is weak
explanation: There are many situations in which one can resort to n of 1 trials. 1. stem: A trial was designed to evaluate the effect of treating post-MI depression using SSRIs or CBT on cardiac events. The primary outcome studied was a composite measure of the occurrence of death, recurrent MI or cardiac failure. All of the following justify using such a composite endpoint except

The treatment will act more or less the same way across various components of the composite measure
Need for huge sample size can be avoided
There is uncertainty about which single end point to choose
Patients consider some component endpoints of the composite measure to be more important than the others
correctAnswer: Patients consider some component endpoints of the composite measure to be more important than the others
explanation: Composite end points (CEPs) capture the number of patients experiencing any one of several adverse events— e.g. death, MI, or hospitalization—as a primary study endpoint. The main reason for employing CEPs is to decrease the necessary sample size and duration of  follow-up. This may be justified especially when there is a paucity of events in any single category and a presumption that treatment will act in more or less the same way across categories of adverse events. But patients almost invariably assign varying importance to different health outcomes (Do you think patients will consider death, recurrent MI and failure in same terms?). Hence, we must not ignore the possible difference of treatment effect on individual component endpoints on the grounds that they share identical patient-importance. Guyatt G Rennie D et al. stem: A randomised controlled trial was conducted in Norway to determine whether a systematic approach to the treatment of pain can reduce agitation in people with moderate to severe dementia living in nursing homes. 352 residents with moderate to severe dementia and clinically significant behavioural disturbances were recruited from 60 clusters (single independent nursing home units) in 18 nursing homes within five municipalities of western Norway. The nursing home units were randomised to use a stepwise protocol for the treatment of pain in eligible subjects for eight weeks with additional follow-up four weeks after the end of treatment (33 clusters; n=175) or to usual treatment (control, 27 clusters; n=177). Sample size was calculated on the basis of clinically meaningful differences in agitation scores after taking into account the expected intracluster correlation and dropout rates. Participants in the intervention group received individual daily treatment of pain for eight weeks according to the stepwise protocol, with paracetamol (acetaminophen), morphine, buprenorphine transdermal patch, or pregabalin. The control group received usual treatment and care. The primary outcome measure was agitation scores on Cohen- Mansfield agitation inventory. Agitation was significantly reduced in the intervention group compared with control group after eight weeks (results shown in the below table): the average reduction in scores for agitation was 17% (treatment effect estimate -7.0, 95% confidence interval -3.7 to -10.3). Treatment of pain was also significantly beneficial for the overall severity of neuropsychiatric symptoms (-9.0, -5.5 to -12.6) and pain (-1.3, -0.8 to -1.7), but the groups did not differ significantly for activities of daily living or cognition. In the intervention group, there was a worsening of scores on the Cohen-Mansfield agitation inventory between week 8 and week 12, after withdrawal of pain treatment. The authors concluded that a systematic approach to the management of pain could alleviate agitation and could reduce the number of unnecessary prescriptions for psychotropic drugs in residents of nursing homes with moderate to severe dementia. What kind of sampling has been used? 
explanation: This study has used a cluster sampling approach for randomisation.

options: Variability induced by different stepwise treatment options
Variability expected among patients in the same nursing home unit
Variability expected between the nursing home units
Variability expected between patients receiving active and control interventions

explanation:
Effective sample size (ESS) is used in place of actual sample size when undertaking power calculations in a cluster randomised trial. Sample size, in general, refers to the number of units of independent participants recruited for a trial. In a cluster RCT, individuals are not recruited but 'clusters' are recruited. So the effective sample size is much smaller than the actual number of individual participants. To calculate ESS, statisticians use a measure called 'variance inflation factor' or 'design effect' which is derived from an intracluster coefficient. (This concept is

very similar to the notion of intraclass correlation coefficient used when studying inter-rater reliability). A high intracluster coefficient will reduce the effective sample size. Intracluster correlation ? refers to the proportion of total variability of the outcome measure (sum of between-cluster and within-cluster variances) attributed to the between-cluster variability. It can vary between 0 and 1. A very high value for ? (close to 1) is bad news, as it suggests that all of the variability is due to between-cluster differences, and the responses within a cluster are highly correlated. In other words, this means that the entire cluster is behaving as a single observational unit (equivalent to just one patient), thus reducing the effective sample size to a value closer to the total number of clusters recruited. The calculation of ? usually requires a pilot study.

A randomized trial of oral antiretroviral therapy was conducted to evaluate the use of antiretroviral treatment as preexposure prophylaxis among HIV-1 –serodiscordant heterosexual couples from Kenya and Uganda. The HIV-1 –seronegative partner in each couple, was randomly assigned to one of the three study regimens — once-daily tenofovir (TDF), combination tenofovir – emtricitabine (TDF –FTC), or matching placebo — and followed monthly for up to 36 months. Of the enrolled 4758 couples 4747 were followed: 1584 randomly assigned to TDF, 1579 to TDF –FTC, and 1584 to placebo. A total of 82 HIV-1 infections occurred in seronegative participants during the study, 17 in the TDF group, 13 in the TDF –FTC group and 52 in the placebo group, indicating a relative reduction of 67% in the incidence of HIV-1 with TDF (95% confidence interval [CI], 44 to 81; P<0.001) and of 75% with TDF –FTC (95% CI, 55 to 87; P<0.001). Protective effects of TDF –FTC and TDF alone against HIV-1 were not significantly different (P=0.23), and both study medications significantly reduced the HIV-1 incidence among both men and women. Eight participants receiving active treatment were found to have been infected with HIV-1 at baseline, and among these, antiretroviral resistance developed in two during the study. The dropouts were highest for placebo group

Probability of HIV-1 infection increases with time
correctAnswer:
Probability of HIV-1 infection increases with time

A cluster RCT was conducted in Germany to analyse the cost-effectiveness of an optimised care model for people with anxiety disorders in primary care (Konig, H.-H. et al. The British Journal of Psychiatry 2009;195:308-317). 46 primary care practices with 389 individuals with anxiety were randomised to intervention (23 practices, 201 participants) or usual care (23 practices, 188 participants). For monetary valuation of resource utilisation, unit costs were determined for all services used and for all medical goods prescribed or privately purchased at 2006 price levels. Informal care provided by relatives and friends was valued by the mean net income per h (Euros 18.30) in Germany. Productivity loss was quantified based on the human capital approach, valuing illness-related work loss days by the mean labour costs per working day (Euros 169) in Germany. A generic health-related quality of life questionnaire called EQ-5D was used for primary outcome determination. It comprises five questions (items) relating to current problems in the dimensions: mobility; self-care; usual activities; pain/discomfort; and anxiety/depression. Quality-adjusted life-years were calculated by weighting the duration of health states by the EQ -5D index. Beck's anxiety inventory was also used to quantify clinical improvement. To analyse the impact of various assumptions made when calculating QALYs and costs, analyses were performed by varying the following parameters: 1. Using German version of EQ-5D instead or British version 2. Using a different scale called EQ -VAS as QALY weights. 3. Calculating indirect costs using a different approach 4. Varying intervention costs by plus and minus 100%. 5. Calculating ICER for only complete cases with no missing values instead of including all in the analysis. Total costs were higher in the intervention group (Euros 4911 v. Euros 3453, P = 0.09). Mean incremental total costs were Euros 1459. Mean incremental QALYs were -0.0042. Mean difference in BAI score at initial follow-up was 3 points, with intervention group doing better than control group, though this result was not significant. The probability of an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio < Euros 50 000 per quality-adjusted life year was below 10%. What is the below graph called? 


explanation: The attached graph is a cost-effectiveness acceptability curve. It is a plot between incremental cost-effectiveness threshold (or willingness to pay) and the probability that the ICER is less than the threshold set (i.e. the chances of cost-effectiveness).

stem: A 77-year-old man falls out of NICE guidelines to prescribe antidementia medications. But he can get the same medications if he lived in France or Canada under their own national guidelines. How can this be explained in terms of the process of guideline production?

Inadequate appraisal of literature took place while drafting NICE guidelines in UK
Different set of research evidences were appraised by the different national bodies
Guidelines are not only based on evidence but also resource availability, values and collective preferences.
correctAnswer: Guidelines are not only based on evidence but also resource availability, values and collective preferences.
explanation: Steps to be followed in producing a treatment recommendation: Defining the decision ( e.g. decision to switch antipsychotics when first episode of psychosis is not controlled even after 12 weeks of treatment) Specify the possible outcomes (control of symptoms, no effect of switch, increase in side effects, noncompliance, occurrence of depression etc). Using available evidence to specify the link between listed  options and outcomes. (Olanzapine causes weight gain, lesser dropout rate for olanzapine and depots, etc.'¦) Incorporate values/value judgements to decide on optimal course of action (Female patient, poor lifestyle - weight gain is an important problem, etc) Consider local circumstances including resource availability and modify action if needed (no depot clinics locally, no CPNs etc). This might explain the differences in recommendation despite appraising same evidence base.
